entries.ff9f5719257e6b7653a87a446058db0bee2d6c20: <div sID="gen18568" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Ezek.10" sID="Ezek.10"/> <div eID="gen18568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18569" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18570" type="x-p"/> The prophet had observed to us (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.4">ch. viii. 4</reference>) that when he was in vision at Jerusalem he saw the same appearance of the glory of God there that he had seen by the river Chebar; now, in this chapter, he gives us some account of the appearance there, as far as was requisite for the clearing up of two further indications of the approaching destruction of Jerusalem, which God here gave the prophet:—I. The scattering of the coals of fire upon the city, which were taken from between the cherubim, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1-Ezek.10.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. The removal of the glory of God from the temple, and its being upon the wing to be gone, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.8-Ezek.10.22">ver. 8-22</reference>. When God goes out from a people all judgments break in upon them.
entries.0b6ce7a329ec42041231f5d0ba6184f077910d6c: <div eID="gen18570" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18569" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Cherubim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18571" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then I looked, and, behold, in the firmament that was above the head of the cherubims there appeared over them as it were a sapphire stone, as the appearance of the likeness of a throne. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he spake unto the man clothed with linen, and said, Go in between the wheels, <hi type="italic">even</hi> under the cherub, and fill thine hand with coals of fire from between the cherubims, and scatter <hi type="italic">them</hi> over the city. And he went in in my sight. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now the cherubims stood on the right side of the house, when the man went in; and the cloud filled the inner court. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went up from the cherub, <hi type="italic">and stood</hi> over the threshold of the house; and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was full of the brightness of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's glory. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the sound of the cherubims' wings was heard <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the outer court, as the voice of the Almighty God when he speaketh. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when he had commanded the man clothed with linen, saying, Take fire from between the wheels, from between the cherubims; then he went in, and stood beside the wheels. <hi type="super">7</hi> And <hi type="italic">one</hi> cherub stretched forth his hand from between the cherubims unto the fire that <hi type="italic">was</hi> between the cherubims, and took <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the hands of <hi type="italic">him that was</hi> clothed with linen: who took <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and went out. <div eID="gen18571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18572" type="x-p"/> To inspire us with a holy awe and dread of God, and to fill us with his fear, we may observe, in this part of the vision which the prophet had, <div eID="gen18572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18573" type="x-p"/> I. The glorious appearance of his majesty. Something of the invisible world is here in the visible, some faint representations of its brightness and beauty, some shadows, but such as are no more to be compared with the truth and substance than a picture with the life; yet here is enough to oblige us all to the utmost reverence in our thoughts of God and approaches to him, if we will but admit the impressions this discovery of him will make. 1. He is here <hi type="italic">in the firmament above the head of the cherubim,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1">v. 1</reference>. He manifests his glory in the upper world, where purity and brightness are both in perfection; and the vast expanse of the firmament aims to speak the God that dwells there infinite. It is <hi type="italic">the firmament of his power</hi> and of his prospect too; for thence <hi type="italic">he beholds</hi> all <hi type="italic">the children of men.</hi> The divine nature infinitely transcends the angelic nature, and God is <hi type="italic">above the head of the cherubim,</hi> in respect not only of his dignity above them, but of his dominion over them. Cherubim have great power, and wisdom, and influence, but they are all subject to God and Christ. 2. He is here upon the throne, or that which had <hi type="italic">the appearance of the likeness of a throne</hi> (for God's glory and government infinitely transcend all the brightest ideas our minds can either form or receive concerning them); and it was <hi type="italic">as it were a sapphire-stone,</hi> pure and sparkling; such a throne has God <hi type="italic">prepared in the heavens,</hi> far exceeding the thrones of any earthly potentates. 3. He is here attended with a glorious train of holy angels. When God came into his temple <hi type="italic">the cherubim stood on the right side of the house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">v. 3</reference>), as the prince's life-guard, attending the gate of his palace. Christ has angels at command. The orders given to all the angels of God are, to <hi type="italic">worship him.</hi> Some observe that they <hi type="italic">stood on the right side of the house,</hi> that is, the south side, because on the north side the image of jealousy was, and other instances of idolatry, from which they would place themselves at as great a distance as might be. 4. The appearance of his glory is veiled with a cloud, and yet out of that cloud darts forth a dazzling lustre; in <hi type="italic">the house</hi> and <hi type="italic">inner court</hi> there was <hi type="italic">a cloud</hi> and darkness, which filled them, and yet either the outer court, or the same court after some time, <hi type="italic">was full of the brightness of the Lord's glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3-Ezek.10.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. There was a darting forth of light and brightness; but if any over curious eye pried into it, it would find itself lost in a cloud. His righteousness is conspicuous <hi type="italic">as the great mountains,</hi> and the brightness of it <hi type="italic">fills the court;</hi> but <hi type="italic">his judgments are a great deep,</hi> which we cannot fathom, <hi type="italic">a cloud</hi> which we cannot see through. <hi type="italic">The brightness</hi> discovers enough to awe and direct our consciences, but the <hi type="italic">cloud</hi> forbids us to expect the gratifying of our curiosity; for <hi type="italic">we cannot order our speech by reasons of darkness.</hi> Thus (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.4">Hab. iii. 4</reference>) <hi type="italic">he had rays coming out of his hand, and yet there was the hiding of his power.</hi> Nothing is more clear than that God <hi type="italic">is,</hi> nothing more dark than <hi type="italic">what</hi> he is. God <hi type="italic">covers himself with light,</hi> and yet, as to us, <hi type="italic">makes darkness his pavilion.</hi> God took possession of the tabernacle and the temple in a cloud, which was always the symbol of his presence. In the temple above there will be no cloud, but we shall see <hi type="italic">face to face.</hi> 5. The cherubim, made a dreadful sound with their wings, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.5">v. 5</reference>. The vibration of them, as of the strings of musical instruments, made a curious melody; bees, and other winged insects, make a noise with their wings. Probably this intimated their preparing to remove, by stretching forth and lifting up their wings, which made this noise as it were to give warning of it. This noise is said to be <hi type="italic">as the voice of the almighty God when he speaks,</hi> as the thunder, which is called <hi type="italic">the voice of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Ps. xxix. 3</reference>), or <hi type="italic">as the voice of the Lord</hi> when he spoke to Israel on Mount Sinai; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he then gave the law with abundance of terror, to signify with what terror he would reckon for the violation of it, which he was now about to do. This noise of their wings <hi type="italic">was heard even to the outer court,</hi> the court of the people; for the Lord's voice, in his judgments, <hi type="italic">cries in the city,</hi> which those may hear that do not, as Ezekiel, see the visions of them. <div eID="gen18573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18574" type="x-p"/> II. The terrible directions of his wrath. This vision has a further tendency than merely to set forth the divine grandeur; further orders are to be given for the destruction of Jerusalem. The greatest devastations are made by fire and sword. For a general slaughter of the inhabitants of Jerusalem orders were given in the foregoing chapter; now here we have a command to lay the city in ashes, by <hi type="italic">scattering coals of fire</hi> upon it, which in the vision were fetched <hi type="italic">from between the cherubim.</hi> <div eID="gen18574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18575" type="x-p"/> 1. For the issuing out of orders to do this <hi type="italic">the glory of the Lord</hi> was lifted <hi type="italic">up from the cherub</hi> (as in the chapter before for the giving of orders there, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">v. 3</reference>) <hi type="italic">and stood</hi> upon <hi type="italic">the threshold of the house,</hi> in imitation of the courts of judgement, which they kept in the gates of their cities. The people would not hear the oracles which God had delivered to them from his holy temple, and therefore they shall thence be made to hear their doom. <div eID="gen18575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18576" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The man clothed in linen</hi> who had marked those that were to be preserved is to be employed in this service; for <hi type="italic">the same Jesus</hi> that is the protector and Saviour of those that believe, having <hi type="italic">all judgement committed to him,</hi> that of condemnation as well as that of absolution, will <hi type="italic">come in a flaming fire to take vengeance on those that obey not his gospel.</hi> He that sits on the throne calls <hi type="italic">to the man clothed in linen</hi> to <hi type="italic">go in between the wheels, and fill his hand with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That the burning of the city and temple by the Chaldeans was a consumption determined, and that therein they executed God's counsel, did what he designed before should be done. (2.) That the fire of divine wrath, which kindles judgement upon a people, is just and holy, for it is fire fetched <hi type="italic">from between the cherubim.</hi> The fire on God's altar, where atonement was made, had been slighted, to avenge which fire is here fetched from heaven, like that by which Nadab and Abihu were killed for offering strange fire. If a city, or town, or house, be burnt, whether by design or accident, if we trace it in its original, we shall find that the <hi type="italic">coals</hi> which kindled the <hi type="italic">fire</hi> came from <hi type="italic">between the wheels;</hi> for there is not any evil of that kind in the city, but the Lord has done it. (3.) That Jesus Christ acts by commission from the Father, for from him he <hi type="italic">receives authority to execute judgement, because he is the Son of man.</hi> Christ came to <hi type="italic">send fire on the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">Luke xii. 49</reference>) and in the great day will speak this world into ashes. By fire from his hand, the earth, and all the works that are therein, will be burnt up. <div eID="gen18576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18577" type="x-p"/> 3. This <hi type="italic">man clothed with linen</hi> readily attended to this service; though, being <hi type="italic">clothed with linen,</hi> he was very unfit to go among the burning <hi type="italic">coals,</hi> yet, being called, he said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come;</hi> this commandment he had received of his Father, and he complied with it; the prophet saw him go in, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">He went in, and stood beside the wheels,</hi> expecting to be furnished there with the coals he was to scatter; for what Christ was to give he first received, whether for mercy or judgement. He was directed to take fire, but he staid till he had it given him, to show how slow he is to execute judgement, and how long-suffering to us-ward. <div eID="gen18577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18578" type="x-p"/> 4. One of the cherubim reached him a handful of fire from the midst of the living creatures. The prophet, when he first saw this vision, observed that there were <hi type="italic">burning coals of fire,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lamps,</hi> that <hi type="italic">went up and down among the living creatures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.13">ch. i. 13</reference>); thence this fire was taken, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.7">v. 7</reference>. The <hi type="italic">spirit of burning, the refiner's fire,</hi> by which Christ purifies his church, is of a divine original. It is by a celestial fire, <hi type="italic">fire</hi> from <hi type="italic">between the cherubim,</hi> that wonders are wrought. <hi type="italic">The cherubim put it into</hi> his <hi type="italic">hand;</hi> for the angels are ready to be employed by the Lord Jesus and to serve all his purposes. <div eID="gen18578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18579" type="x-p"/> 5. When he had taken the fire he <hi type="italic">went out,</hi> no doubt to <hi type="italic">scatter</hi> it up and down upon <hi type="italic">the city,</hi> as he was directed. And <hi type="italic">who can abide the day of his coming?</hi> Who can stand before him when he goes out in his anger?
entries.7a5e07832b51d586dd06ad158a3944ec28efd3bf: <div eID="gen18579" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Divine Glory. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18580" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And there appeared in the cherubims the form of a man's hand under their wings. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when I looked, behold the four wheels by the cherubims, one wheel by one cherub, and another wheel by another cherub: and the appearance of the wheels <hi type="italic">was</hi> as the colour of a beryl stone. <hi type="super">10</hi> And <hi type="italic">as for</hi> their appearances, they four had one likeness, as if a wheel had been in the midst of a wheel. <hi type="super">11</hi> When they went, they went upon their four sides; they turned not as they went, but to the place whither the head looked they followed it; they turned not as they went. <hi type="super">12</hi> And their whole body, and their backs, and their hands, and their wings, and the wheels, <hi type="italic">were</hi> full of eyes round about, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the wheels that they four had. <hi type="super">13</hi> As for the wheels, it was cried unto them in my hearing, O wheel. <hi type="super">14</hi> And every one had four faces: the first face <hi type="italic">was</hi> the face of a cherub, and the second face <hi type="italic">was</hi> the face of a man, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the cherubims were lifted up. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the living creature that I saw by the river of Chebar. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when the cherubims went, the wheels went by them: and when the cherubims lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the same wheels also turned not from beside them. <hi type="super">17</hi> When they stood, <hi type="italic">these</hi> stood; and when they were lifted up, <hi type="italic">these</hi> lifted up themselves <hi type="italic">also:</hi> for the spirit of the living creature <hi type="italic">was</hi> in them. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> departed from off the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubims. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the cherubims lifted up their wings, and mounted up from the earth in my sight: when they went out, the wheels also <hi type="italic">were</hi> beside them, and <hi type="italic">every one</hi> stood at the door of the east gate of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house; and the glory of the God of Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> over them above. <hi type="super">20</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the living creature that I saw under the God of Israel by the river of Chebar; and I knew that they <hi type="italic">were</hi> the cherubims. <hi type="super">21</hi> Every one had four faces apiece, and every one four wings; and the likeness of the hands of a man <hi type="italic">was</hi> under their wings. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the likeness of their faces <hi type="italic">was</hi> the same faces which I saw by the river of Chebar, their appearances and themselves: they went every one straight forward. <div eID="gen18580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18581" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of the vision of God's glory which Ezekiel saw, here intended to introduce that direful omen of the departure of that glory from them, which would open the door for ruin to break in. <div eID="gen18581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18582" type="x-p"/> I. Ezekiel sees the glory of God shining in the sanctuary, as he had seen it <hi type="italic">by the river of Chebar,</hi> and gives an account of it, that those who had by their wickedness provoked God to depart from them might know what they had lost and might lament after the Lord, groaning out their Ichabod, <hi type="italic">Where is the glory?</hi> Ezekiel here sees the operations of divine Providence in the government of the lower world, and the affairs of it, represented by the <hi type="italic">four wheels;</hi> and the perfections of the holy angels, the inhabitants of the upper world, and their ministrations, represented by the <hi type="italic">four living creatures,</hi> every one of which had <hi type="italic">four faces.</hi> The agency of the angels in directing the affairs of this world is represented by the close communication that was between the <hi type="italic">living creatures</hi> and the <hi type="italic">wheels,</hi> the wheels being guided by them in all their motions, as the chariot is by him that drives it. But the same Spirit being both in the <hi type="italic">living creatures</hi> and in the <hi type="italic">wheels</hi> denoted the infinite wisdom which serves its own purposes by the ministration of angels and all the occurrences of this lower world. So that this vision gives out faith a view of that throne which the Lord has <hi type="italic">prepared in the heavens,</hi> and that kingdom of which <hi type="italic">rules over all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">Ps. ciii. 19</reference>. The prophet observes that this was <hi type="italic">the same vision</hi> with that he saw by the river of Chebar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.15">v. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.22">22</reference>), and yet in one thing there seems to be a material difference, that that which was there <hi type="italic">was the face of an ox,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">on the left side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.10">ch. i. 10</reference>), is here the <hi type="italic">face of a cherub,</hi> and is the <hi type="italic">first face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.14">v. 14</reference>), whence some have concluded that the peculiar face of a cherub was that of an ox, which the Israelites had an eye to when they made the golden calf. I rather think that in this latter vision the first face was the proper appearance or figure of a cherub, which Ezekiel knew very well, being a priest, by what he had seen in the temple of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.29">1 Kings vi. 29</reference>), but which we now have no certainty of at all; and by this Ezekiel knew assuredly, whereas before he only conjectured it, that they were all cherubim, though putting on different faces, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.20">v. 20</reference>. And this first appearing in the proper figure of a cherub, and yet it being proper to retain the number of four, that of the ox is left out and dropped, because the face of the cherub had been most abused by the worship of an ox. As sometimes when God appeared to deliver his people, so now when he appeared to depart from them, <hi type="italic">he rode on a cherub, and did fly.</hi> Now observe here, 1. That this world is subject to turns, and changes, and various revolutions. The course of affairs in it is represented by <hi type="italic">wheels</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.9">v. 9</reference>); sometimes one spoke is uppermost and sometimes another; they are still ebbing and flowing like the sea, waxing and waning like the moon, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4">1 Sam. ii. 4</reference>, &c. Nay, their appearance is as if there were a <hi type="italic">wheel in the midst of a wheel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.10">v. 10</reference>), which intimates the mutual references of providence to each other, their dependences on each other, and the joint tendency of all to one common end, while their motions as to us are intricate, and perplexed, and seemingly contrary. 2. That there is an admirable harmony and uniformity in the various occurrences of providence (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">As for the wheels,</hi> though they moved several ways, yet <hi type="italic">it was cried to them, O wheel!</hi> they were all as one, being guided by one Spirit to one end; for God works all according to the counsel of his own will, which is one, for his own glory, which is one. And this makes the disposal of Providence truly admirable, and to be looked upon with wonder. As the works of his creation, considered separately, were <hi type="italic">good,</hi> but all together <hi type="italic">very good,</hi> so the wheels of Providence, considered by themselves, are wonderful, but put them together and they are very wonderful. <hi type="italic">O wheel!</hi> 3. That the motions of Providence are steady and regular, and whatever the Lord pleases that he does and is never put upon new counsels. <hi type="italic">The wheels turned not as they went</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.11">v. 11</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">living creatures went every one straight forward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.22">v. 22</reference>. Whatever difficulties lay in their way, they were sure to get over them, and were never obliged to stand still, turn aside, or go back. So perfectly known to God are all his works that he never put upon to new counsels. 4. That God makes more use of the ministration of angels in the government of this lower world than we are aware of: <hi type="italic">The four wheels were by the cherubim, one wheel by one cherub and another wheel by another cherub,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.9">v. 9</reference>. What has been imagined by some concerning the spheres above, that every orb has its intelligence to guide it, is here intimated concerning the wheels below, that every wheel has its cherub to guide it. We think it a satisfaction to us if under the wise God there are wise men employed in managing the affairs of the kingdoms and churches; whether there be so or no, it appears by this that there are wise angels employed, <hi type="italic">a cherub to every wheel.</hi> 5. That all the motions of Providence and all the ministrations of angels are under the government of the great God. They are all <hi type="italic">full of eyes,</hi> those eyes of the Lord which run to and fro through the earth and which the angels have always an eye to, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.12">v. 12</reference>. The <hi type="italic">living creatures</hi> and <hi type="italic">the wheels</hi> concur in their motions and rests (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.17">v. 17</reference>); for <hi type="italic">the Spirit of life,</hi> as it may be read, or <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the living creatures, is in the wheels.</hi> The Spirit of God directs all the creatures, both upper and lower, so as to make them serve the divine purpose. Events are not determined by the <hi type="italic">wheel of fortune,</hi> which is blind, but by the <hi type="italic">wheels of Providence,</hi> which are full of eyes. <div eID="gen18582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18583" type="x-p"/> II. Ezekiel sees the glory of God removing out of the sanctuary, the place where God's honour had long dwelt, and this sight is as sad as the other was grateful. It was pleasant to see that God had not <hi type="italic">forsaken the earth</hi> (as the idolaters suggested, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">ch. ix. 9</reference>), but sad to see that he was forsaking his sanctuary. The <hi type="italic">glory of the Lord stood over the threshold,</hi> having thence given the necessary orders for the destruction of the city, and it <hi type="italic">stood over the cherubim,</hi> not those in the most holy place, but those that Ezekiel now saw in vision, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">v. 18</reference>. It ascended that stately chariot, as the judge, when he comes off the bench, goes into his coach and is gone. And immediately <hi type="italic">the cherubim lifted up their wings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">v. 19</reference>), as they were directed, and they <hi type="italic">mounted up from the earth,</hi> as birds upon the wing; and, <hi type="italic">when they went out,</hi> the wheels of this chariot were not drawn, but went by instinct, <hi type="italic">beside them,</hi> by which it appeared that <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.</hi> Thus, when God is leaving a people in displeasure, angels above, and all events here below, shall concur to further his departure. But observe here, In the courts of the temple where the people of Israel had dishonoured their God, had cast off his yoke and withdrawn the shoulder from it, blessed angels appear very ready to serve him, to draw in his chariot, and to <hi type="italic">mount upwards</hi> with it. God has shown the prophet how the will of God was disobeyed by men on earth (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1-Ezek.8.18">ch. viii.</reference>); here he shows him how readily it is obeyed by angels and inferior creatures; and it is a comfort to us, when we grieve for the wickedness of the wicked, to think how his angels do his commandments, <hi type="italic">hearkening to the voice of his word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.20">Ps. ciii. 20</reference>. Let us now, 1. Take a view of this chariot in which <hi type="italic">the glory of the God of Israel rides triumphantly.</hi> He that is the God of Israel is the God of heaven and earth, and has the command of all the powers of both. Let the faithful Israelites comfort themselves with this, that he who is their God is above the cherubim; their Redeemer is so (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Pet. iii. 22</reference>) and has the sole and sovereign disposal of all events; <hi type="italic">the living creatures</hi> and <hi type="italic">the wheels</hi> agree to serve him, so that he is <hi type="italic">head over all things to the church.</hi> The rabbin call this vision that Ezekiel had <hi type="italic">Mercabah</hi>—the <hi type="italic">vision of the chariot;</hi> and thence they call the more abstruse part of divinity, which treats concerning God and spirits, <hi type="italic">Opus currus</hi>—<hi type="italic">The work of the chariot,</hi> as they do the other part, that is more plain and familiar, <hi type="italic">Opus bereshith</hi>—<hi type="italic">The work of the creation.</hi>—2. Let us attend the motions of this chariot: The <hi type="italic">cherubim, and the glory of God above them, stood at the door of the east gate of the Lord's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">v. 19</reference>. But observe with how many stops and pauses God departs, as loth to go, as if to see if there be any that will intercede with him to return. None of the priests in the inner court, between the temple and the altar, would court his stay; therefore he leaves their court, and stands at the <hi type="italic">east gate,</hi> which led into the <hi type="italic">court of the people,</hi> to see if any of them would yet at length stand in the gap. Note, God removes by degrees from a provoking people; and, when he is ready to depart in displeasure, would return to them in mercy if they were but a repenting praying people.  <chapter eID="Ezek.10"/> <div eID="gen18583" type="x-p"/>

entries.48a18f4979a29fc36eac00b66f96be1ea4ac8767: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11095"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1-Ezek.10.22">Eze 10:1-22</reference>. Vision of Coals of Fire Scattered over the City:</title> <div sID="gen19994" type="x-p"/> Repetition of the Vision of the Cherubim.<div eID="gen19994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11095"/>1. The throne of Jehovah appearing in the midst of the judgments implies that whatever intermediate agencies be employed, He controls them, and that the whole flows as a necessary consequence from His essential holiness (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.22">Eze 1:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen19995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cherubim--</hi>in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.5">Eze 1:5</reference>, called "living creatures." The repetition of the vision implies that the judgments are approaching nearer and nearer. These two visions of Deity were granted in the beginning of Ezekiel's career, to qualify him for witnessing to God's glory amidst his God-forgetting people and to stamp truth on his announcements; also to signify the removal of God's manifestation from the visible temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>) for a long period (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>). The feature (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.12">Eze 10:12</reference>) mentioned as to the cherubim that they were "full of eyes," though omitted in the former vision, is not a difference, but a more specific detail observed by Ezekiel now on closer inspection. Also, here, there is no rainbow (the symbol of mercy after the flood of wrath) as in the former; for here judgment is the prominent thought, though the marking of the remnant in <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Eze 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">6</reference> shows that there was mercy in the background. The cherubim, perhaps, represent redeemed humanity combining in and with itself the highest forms of subordinate creaturely life (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Ro 8:20</reference>). Therefore they are associated with the twenty-four elders and are distinguished from the angels (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.1-Rev.5.14">Re 5:1-14</reference>). They stand on the mercy seat of the ark, and on that ground become the habitation of God from which His glory is to shine upon the world. The different forms symbolize the different phases of the Church. So the quadriform Gospel, in which the incarnate Saviour has lodged the revelation of Himself in a fourfold aspect, and from which His glory shines on the Christian world, answers to the emblematic throne from which He shone on the Jewish Church. <div eID="gen19996" type="x-p"/>
entries.07bd590d5c15f432ea164e2fb8f492ed377234c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11096"/><div sID="gen19997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11096"/><hi type="bold">2. he--</hi>Jehovah; He who sat on the "throne."<div eID="gen19997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man--</hi>the Messenger of mercy becoming the Messenger of judgment (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>). Human agents of destruction shall fulfil the will of "the Man," who is Lord of men.<div eID="gen19998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels--</hi>Hebrew, galgal, implying quick revolution; so the impetuous onset of the foe (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">Eze 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.10">26:10</reference>); whereas "ophan," in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.15">Eze 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference> implies mere revolution.<div eID="gen19999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coals of fire--</hi>the wrath of God about to burn the city, as His sword had previously slain its guilty inhabitants. This "fire," how different from the fire on the altar never going out (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.12">Le 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">13</reference>), whereby, in type, peace was made with God! Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">Is 33:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">14</reference>. It is therefore not taken from the altar of reconciliation, but from between the wheels of the cherubim, representing the providence of God, whereby, and not by chance, judgment is to fall. <div eID="gen20000" type="x-p"/>
entries.18d1d15deeac6a05735f460d746aef12fd5b27a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11097"/><div sID="gen20001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11097"/><hi type="bold">3. right ... of ... house--</hi>The scene of the locality whence judgment emanates is the temple, to mark God's vindication of His holiness injured there. The cherubim here are not those in the holy of holies, for the latter had not "wheels." They stood on "the right of the house," that is, the south, for the Chaldean power, guided by them, had already advanced from the north (the direction of Babylon), and had destroyed the men in the temple, and was now proceeding to destroy the city, which lay south and west.<div eID="gen20001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the cherubim ... the man--</hi>There was perfect concert of action between the cherubic representative of the angels and "the Man," to minister to whom they "stood" there (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.7">Eze 10:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cloud--</hi>emblem of God's displeasure; as the "glory" or "brightness" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>) typifies His majesty and clearness in judgment. <div eID="gen20003" type="x-p"/>
entries.08a4d72d876c7ab1bfde08a00ff0563f2b7daf35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11098"/><div sID="gen20004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11098"/>4. The court outside was full of the Lord's brightness, while it was only the cloud that filled the house inside, the scene of idolatries, and therefore of God's displeasure. God's throne was on the threshold. The temple, once filled with brightness, is now darkened with cloud. <div eID="gen20004" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b725c990b5d1543ae762bb502506098b79a5406: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11099"/><div sID="gen20005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11099"/><hi type="bold">5. sound of ... wings--</hi>prognostic of great and awful changes.<div eID="gen20005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">voice of ... God--</hi>the thunder (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.3">Psa 29:3</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen20006" type="x-p"/>
entries.86235c42e7a843d7b2e5f349cd4264cc30ed54c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11100"/><div sID="gen20007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11100"/><hi type="bold">6. went in--</hi>not into the temple, but between the cherubim. Ezekiel sets aside the Jews' boast of the presence of God with them. The cherubim, once the ministers of grace, are now the ministers of vengeance. When "commanded," He without delay obeys (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">Psa 40:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.7">He 10:7</reference>). <div eID="gen20007" type="x-p"/>
entries.14d0543f0d4bd0a4334a41942c18f43dc1e6d3d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11101"/><div sID="gen20008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11101"/>7. See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">Eze 10:3</reference>.<div eID="gen20008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one cherub--</hi>one of the four cherubim.<div eID="gen20009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his hand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.8">Eze 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went out--</hi>to burn the city. <div eID="gen20011" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6bad8b90a4ac3c32e2279dbe1ea2aa6ee42f00d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11102"/><div sID="gen20012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11102"/>8. The "wings" denote alacrity, the "hands" efficacy and aptness, in executing the functions assigned to them. <div eID="gen20012" type="x-p"/>
entries.e76fe1190ff20c74ae08e21699247e122bc0d8d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11103"/><div sID="gen20013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11103"/><hi type="bold">9. wheels--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.15">Eze 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>). The things which, from <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.8">Eze 10:8</reference> to the end of the chapter, are repeated from the first chapter are expressed more decidedly, now that he gets a nearer view: the words "as it were," and "as if," so often occurring in the first chapter, are therefore mostly omitted. The "wheels" express the manifold changes and revolutions in the world; also that in the chariot of His providence God transports the Church from one place to another and everywhere can preserve it; a truth calculated to alarm the people in Jerusalem and to console the exiles [Polanus]. <div eID="gen20013" type="x-p"/>
entries.30fa60d130e66152a1f7b22792821fb6d521b7df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11104"/><div sID="gen20014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11104"/><hi type="bold">10. four had one likeness--</hi>In the wonderful variety of God's works there is the greatest harmony:--<div eID="gen20014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20015" type="x-p"/> "In human works, though labored on with pain,<div eID="gen20015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20016" type="x-p"/> One thousand movements scarce one purpose gain;<div eID="gen20016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20017" type="x-p"/> In God's one single doth its end produce,<div eID="gen20017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20018" type="x-p"/> Yet serves to second, too, some other use.<div eID="gen20018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20019" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.16">Eze 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen20019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheel ... in ... a wheel--</hi>cutting one another at fight angles, so that the whole might move in any of the four directions or quarters of the world. God's doings, however involved they seem to us, cohere, so that lower causes subserve the higher. <div eID="gen20020" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3a8cc3d8cac57f1682ade9b0d75d971d261eed9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11105"/><div sID="gen20021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11105"/>11. (See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.17">Eze 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen20021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turned not--</hi>without accomplishing their course (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Is 55:11</reference>) [Grotius]. Rather, "they moved straight on without turning" (so <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.9">Eze 1:9</reference>). Having a face towards each of the four quarters, they needed not to turn around when changing their direction.<div eID="gen20022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whither ... head looked--</hi>that is, "whither the head" of the animal cherub-form, belonging to and directing each wheel, "looked," thither the wheel "followed." The wheels were not guided by some external adventitious impetus, but by some secret divine impulse of the cherubim themselves. <div eID="gen20023" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3dc5ffeb9e7d01de6fe2bf409d0cdbd0e6a00fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11106"/><div sID="gen20024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11106"/><hi type="bold">12. body--</hi>literally, "flesh," because a body consists of flesh.<div eID="gen20024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels ... full of eyes--</hi>The description (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.18">Eze 1:18</reference>) attributes eyes to the "wheels" alone; here there is added, on closer observation, that the cherubim themselves had them. The "eyes" imply that God, by His wisdom, beautifully reconciles seeming contrarieties (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Ch 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">Pr 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zec 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen20025" type="x-p"/>
entries.4415a976b5cbe4b65c9a8c8c14a7a1f18bc368b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11107"/><div sID="gen20026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11107"/><hi type="bold">13. O wheel--</hi>rather, "they were called, whirling," that is, they were most rapid in their revolutions [Maurer]; or, better, "It was cried unto them, The whirling" [Fairbairn]. Galgal here used for "wheel," is different from ophan, the simple word for "wheel." Galgal is the whole wheelwork machinery with its whirlwind-like rotation. Their being so addressed is in order to call them immediately to put themselves in rapid motion. <div eID="gen20026" type="x-p"/>
entries.e03de97cb16491c8cb83ff136acddf6e23bc6fcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11108"/><div sID="gen20027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11108"/><hi type="bold">14. cherub--</hi>but in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.10">Eze 1:10</reference> it is an ox. The chief of the four cherubic forms was not the ox, but man. Therefore "cherub" cannot be synonymous with "ox." Probably Ezekiel, standing in front of one of the cherubim (namely, that which handed the coals to the man in linen), saw of him, not merely the ox-form, but the whole fourfold form, and therefore calls him simply "cherub"; whereas of the other three, having only a side view, he specifies the form of each which met his eye [Fairbairn]. As to the likelihood of the lower animals sharing in "the restoration of all things," see <reference osisRef="Isa.11.6">Is 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">65:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Ro 8:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">21</reference>; this accords with the animal forms combined with the human to typify redeemed man. <div eID="gen20027" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e81f311dc92a3e4417c6df093968fdde9299bd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11109"/><div sID="gen20028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11109"/>15. The repeated declaration of the identity of the vision with that at the Chebar is to arouse attention to it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.22">Eze 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.23">3:23</reference>).<div eID="gen20028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the living creature--</hi>used collectively, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.17">Eze 10:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.20">20</reference>; 1:20. <div eID="gen20029" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed410364cc26f372932ac91a7bffff1941a094b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11110"/><div sID="gen20030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11110"/>16. (See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.11">Eze 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.19">Eze 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen20030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifted up ... wings--</hi>to depart, following "the glory of the Lord" which was on the point of departing (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>). <div eID="gen20031" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f80f8c4db2a3088178ae24e986a3336f8c9ae13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11111"/><div sID="gen20032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11111"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.12">Eze 1:12</reference>, 20, 21).<div eID="gen20032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood--</hi>God never stands still (<reference osisRef="John.5.17">Joh 5:17</reference>), therefore neither do the angels; but to human perceptions He seems to do so. <div eID="gen20033" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c46f6a07175e0b902ba32cd14edc6b4a3efbbd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11112"/><div sID="gen20034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11112"/>18. The departure of the symbol of God's presence from the temple preparatory to the destruction of the city. Foretold in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">De 31:17</reference>. Woe be to those from whom God departs (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.12">Ho 9:12</reference>)! Compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.21">4:21</reference>: "I-chabod, Thy glory is departed." Successive steps are marked in His departure; so slowly and reluctantly does the merciful God leave His house. First He leaves the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3">Eze 9:3</reference>); He elevates His throne above the threshold of the house (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1">Eze 10:1</reference>); leaving the cherubim He sits on the throne (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>); He and the cherubim, after standing for a time at the door of the east gate (where was the exit to the lower court of the people), leave the house altogether (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">19</reference>), not to return till <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>. <div eID="gen20034" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6301931c09277e24089f8cd1dcbfcffab8209ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11113"/><div sID="gen20035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11113"/><hi type="bold">20. I knew ... cherubim--</hi>By the second sight of the cherubim, he learned to identify them with the angelic forms situated above the ark of the covenant in the temple, which as a priest, he "knew" about from the high priest. <div eID="gen20035" type="x-p"/>
entries.9221c62edb7f8bacf7bc1540d14c1cc92ac90efd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11114"/><div sID="gen20036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11114"/>21. The repetition is in order that the people about to live without the temple might have, instead, the knowledge of the temple mysteries, thus preparing them for a future restoration of the covenant. So perverse were they that they would say, "Ezekiel fancies he saw what has no existence." He, therefore, repeats it over and over again. <div eID="gen20036" type="x-p"/>
entries.b076a82095e41470395173aaf72d37dcaad7d0e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11115"/><div sID="gen20037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11115"/><hi type="bold">22. straight forward--</hi>intent upon the object they aimed at, not deviating from the way nor losing sight of the end (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.52">Lu 9:52</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.10"/>

entries.caa2c831cc969995486a75e272dde78c40ab1734: <div eID="gen31442" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31443" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31444" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31444" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31443" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31445" type="x-p"/> The same august vision which appeared to the prophet at first, is repeated here; and coals of fire are scattered over the city to intimate that it was to be burned. The symbol of the Divine presence is likewise represented as removing farther and farther from the temple, to signify that God's protection was about to be withdrawn from it, vv. 1-22. It may not be improper to remark, that whatever is particularly intended by the cherubim, wheels, firmament, throne, etc., described in this and the first chapter, the prophet several times informs us (<reference osisRef="Eze.1.28">Eze 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.3.25">Eze 3:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.8.4">Eze 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.10.18">Eze 10:18</reference>), that his vision was a manifestation or similitude of the Glory of Jehovah; or, in other words, consisted of a set of hieroglyphics by which this glory was in some measure represented. It is also worthy of observation, that the faces of the living creatures, of which we have an account in the fourth chapter of the Apocalypse, are precisely the same with those of Ezekiel's cherubim; and we nay readily collect, as Mr. Mede remarks, the quarter of the heavens in which each cherub was situated in reference to the other three, from the consideration that as Ezekiel saw the vision proceeding from the North, (see <reference osisRef="Eze.1.4">Eze 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.1.10">Eze 1:10</reference>), the human face of the cherubim was towards him, or the south; on his right hand, or the east, was the face of a lion; on his left hand, or the west, the face of an ox; and towards the north, the face of an eagle. <div eID="gen31445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31446" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31447" type="x-p"/> As it were a sapphire stone - See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.1.22-Eze.1.26">Eze 1:22-26</reference> (note). The chariot, here mentioned by the prophet, was precisely the same as that which he saw at the river Chebar, as himself tells us, <reference osisRef="Eze.1.15">Eze 1:15</reference>, of which see the description in Ezekiel 1.
entries.83686bc40a8addd3a2e94a92b858605af390baa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31448" type="x-p"/> Coals of fire - These were to signify the burning of the city by the Chaldeans. It seems that the space between the four wheels, which was all on fire, was that from which those coals were taken.
entries.d09e3da6fbe2c956fe84670e24e5f95d707e4cec: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31449" type="x-p"/> On the right side of the house - The right hand always marked the south among the Hebrews.
entries.db7682af57030f3dd3210a9e77d55af7e3defd58: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31450" type="x-p"/> The glory of the Lord went up - This is repeated from <reference osisRef="Eze.9.3">Eze 9:3</reference>. <div eID="gen31450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31451" type="x-p"/> The house was filled with the cloud - This is a fact similar to what occurred frequently at the tabernacle in the wilderness, and in the dedication of the temple by Solomon. What is mentioned here was the Divine shechinah, the symbolical representation of the majesty of God.
entries.c603ee940c01e459c63744aa0e9ddd1ec616c51a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31452" type="x-p"/> As the voice of the Almighty God - That is, as thunder; for this was called the voice of God.
entries.d28d9b7ea198c27991b0f346fdcb5eba3c7451e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31453" type="x-p"/> The form of a man's hand under their wings - I am still of opinion that the hands and wings were not distinct. The arms were feathered like wings, and the hand terminated the arm; but as the long front feathers of the wings would extend much beyond the fingers, hence the hands would appear to be under the wings. See on <reference osisRef="Eze.1.8">Eze 1:8</reference> (note). The human hand might be intended to show that God helps and punishes man by man; and that, in the general operations of his providence, he makes use of human agency.
entries.6a8a17edd16d0b21158bbbaa5b974f832625a63d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31454" type="x-p"/> The color of a beryl stone - אבן תרשיש eben Tarshish, "the stone of Tarshish." The Vulgate translates it chrysolith; Symmachus, the jacinct; the Septuagint, the carbuncle. In the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Eze.1.16">Eze 1:16</reference>, it is כעין תרשיש keeyn Tarshish, "like the eye of Tarshish;" i.e., the color of tarshish, or the stone so called, which the Vulgate translates visio maris, "like the sea," i.e., azure. The beryl is a gem of a green color, passing from one side into blue, on the other side into yellow. The chrysolith is also green, what is called pistachio green; but the chrysolith of the ancients was our topaz, which is of a fine wine yellow. The beryl, or chrysolith, is most likely what is here meant by tarshish. One name among the ancients served for several kinds of gems that were nearly of the same color. The moderns go more by chemical characters than by color.
entries.279891bc1aa915f14c314399432e1a389f3a1d07: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31455" type="x-p"/> A wheel had been in the midst of a wheel - It is difficult to comprehend this description. It is generally supposed to mean one wheel within another, cutting each other at right angles. This, in my opinion, will not account for the motions attributed to these wheels; nor can I see how, on this supposition, they could have any motion; for if one was moved on its axis, the other must be dragged contrary to its axis. I have conjectured it rather to mean a wheel within a wheel, or a wheel with two rims, working on the same axis. See on <reference osisRef="Eze.1.16-Eze.1.18">Eze 1:16-18</reference> (note). It is however no matter of faith; and the reader may judge as he thinks proper. For other matters relative to this chariot, wheels, cherubim, wings, etc., I must refer to the notes on the first chapter. And perhaps from the whole of this vision and its difficulties, he will see the propriety of the council of rabbins ordering Rabbi Ananias three hundred barrels of oil to light his lamp during the time it would be necessary for him to employ in explaining this one vision.
entries.be0d2a76066e87b1b2268a8bc12da83b77562e6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31456" type="x-p"/> As for the wheels, it was cried unto them - O wheel - Never was there a more unfortunate and unmeaning translation. The word הגלגל haggalgal, may signify, simply, the roller, or a chariot, or roll on, or the swift roller. And he clepide ilke wheelis volible, or turninge about. Old MS. Bible. Any of these will do: "and as to the wheels," לאופנים laophannim, "they were called in my hearing" הגלגל haggalgal, "the chariot." The gentleman who took for his text "O wheel!" and made God's decree of eternal predestination out of it, must have borrowed some of Rabbi Ananias's three hundred barrels of oil! But such working of God's word cannot be too severely reprehended. <div eID="gen31456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31457" type="x-p"/> As these wheels are supposed to represent Divine Providence, bringing about the designs of the Most thigh, how like is the above הגלגל haggalgal, taken as a verb, "roll on," to those words of Virgil in his Pollio: - <div eID="gen31457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31458" type="x-p"/> Talia saela, suis dixerunt, currite, fusis, <div eID="gen31458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31459" type="x-p"/> Concordes stabili fatorum numine Parcae. "The Fates, when they this happy web have spun, <div eID="gen31459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31460" type="x-p"/> Shall bless the sacred clue, and bid it swiftly run."
entries.fdf9d3e319c2887619d56107e21d96d5fb39c685: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31461" type="x-p"/> The first - was the face of a cherub - In <reference osisRef="Eze.1.10">Eze 1:10</reference>, this is called the "face of an ox;" here, the "face of a cherub:" hence, a cherub was in the likeness of an ox, at least, as to its head. כרוב kerub never occurs as a verb; and its meaning cannot be precisely ascertained. Parkhurst thinks the כ caph to be here the note of similitude; and then translates כ ke, "like," רב rab or רוב rob, "the mighty one;" and, in consequence, makes the cherubim an emblem of the Holy Trinity. See his lengthy Dissertation under כרב in his Hebrew and English Lexicon.
entries.085980ee144477268143760132613ecb8d72d10b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen31461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31462" type="x-p"/> And I knew that they were the cherubims - This formation of the plural is quite improper. In general, Hebrew nouns of the masculine gender end in ים im, in the plural; the s, therefore, should never be added to such. Cherub is singular; cherubim is plural. The s should be uniformly expunged. <div eID="gen31462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31463" type="x-p"/> I have already referred to the end of this chapter for farther information relative to this glorious chariot of Jehovah; but I must say that I have met with nothing on the subject that entirely satisfies myself. In the preceding notes I have endeavored to make the literal meaning as plain as possible; and have occasionally given some intimations relative to the general design of this sublime vision. My readers are already apprised that I do not like conjectures on Divine things; many points, that had originally no other origin, are now incorporated with creeds of which it is deemed sinful to doubt. Because some learned and pious men have written to prove that this symbolical compound figure is a representation of the Holy Trinity; therefore, the sentiment now passes current. Now this is not proved; and I suppose never can be proved. The continuator of the Historical Discourses of Saurin has made some sensible remarks on the subject of this vision; and these I shall lay here before the intelligent reader. They deserve attention. <div eID="gen31463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31464" type="x-p"/> This intelligent writer observes: "For the right interpretation of this vision, the following rules should be laid down: - "The first rule is this: - An explanation, which accounts for all the parts contained in the vision, is much more probable than those which explain only one part. "The second is this: - An explanation which is conformable to the present circumstances of the prophet, and of the people to whom he is sent, as well as to the nature of the things which he is called upon to say to them, is incomparably more probable than those explanations which go in quest of past or future events, which have no connection with the immediate circumstances of the prophet, nor with the end of his mission. These rules, which appear incontestable, being laid down, we observe, that their opinion who think that God here draws out a plan of the government of his providence, applied to the present state of the Jews, accounts for all that Ezekiel saw; and that in a manner which refers to the end of the prophet's mission, and all that he had to say to this rebellious people. Why wish God to represent to his prophet the future state of the Christian Church, which was not to be founded till after a series of time, rather than the state of the Jewish Church, and the chastisements which hung over the heads of that hardened people? The people having revolted from God, and persevering obstinately in that revolt, notwithstanding the menaces of the prophet, it was proper to show to Ezekiel, in order that he might declare it to the rebellious, that Providence had its eyes open to all that had been done, all that had hitherto happened, and that it had seized upon the rod to smite. The people imagined, but too much according to the errors of infidelity, that God saw every thing with indifference and had given the world up to chance. It was necessary, therefore, to divest them of these fatal prejudices; and to teach them that the Supreme Being did not behold with the same eye order and disorder, contempt of his laws and submission to his will; and that all the revolutions of states are directed by a superior intelligence, which cannot be imposed upon. The Jewish people imagined but too much that the prophets exaggerated when they threatened them with the severest chastisements. They repeated with emphasis and complacency the promises of God made to the patriarchs; that their posterity should not only be more numerous than the stars of heaven, and the sand which covers the sea-shore; but that it should subsist for ever and ever. God had declared to Abraham, 'I will establish my covenant between me and thee, and thy seed after thee, in their generations, for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee and thy seed after thee,' <reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Gen 17:7</reference>. It was proper, therefore, to show this stiff-necked people that the threatenings of God and his promises were not contradictory. That the people, conformable to the promises given by God to the patriarchs, should not be destroyed; but that, notwithstanding, they should be severely chastised, to correct them for their propensity to idolatry, and their scandalous irregularities. "These suppositions, which are reasonable, being granted, we shall have no difficulty to perceive the sense of this celebrated vision. We shall not follow the order observed by Ezekiel, in the description of what he saw; he raises himself from the nearest to the most distant objects, going back from effects to their general cause. We will begin with the First Cause which gives motion to all that happens, traces out the plan, and procures the execution, according to the rules of his ineffable wisdom, and agreeably to the nature of those creatures which are the object of his agency. Next, we will proceed to consider the effects of this universal Providence, and the intelligent secondary causes which he frequently employs in the administration of the government of the universe. "'Ezekiel saw a firmament which was above the heads of the animals; there was the resemblance of a throne like a sapphire stone; and over the resemblance of the throne, there was, as it were, the resemblance of a man.' This vast transparent firmament represents to us the heaven, the peculiar residence of the Lord of the earth; and where he hath established the throne of his empire. This 'appearance of a man' was the emblem of Providence or God; considered as taking care of all the creatures whom he hath made. Man is the symbol of intelligence. The mind of man, with respect to his knowledge and wisdom, is a weak sketch of that mind which knows all things, and whose wisdom is unbounded. And yet, of all sublunary beings, there is none that approaches so near to the Divine nature as man. Under this emblem also it is that God, considered as seeing all things and directing all, would be represented. This resemblance of man was seated upon a throne to show that God governs all things as Lord and that without agitation and without labor. "The shining metal, and the fire which surrounded him who sat on the throne, were the symbol of his glory and his judgments, which are poured upon the wicked as a fire which nothing can withstand; agreeably to Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa 33:14</reference>. "The Jews acknowledged that there was a Providence which governs the whole universe with infinite wisdom. The psalmist gives us a description of it, equally just and pathetic, in <reference osisRef="Psa.104.27">Psa 104:27</reference>, etc. Christians, no less than Jews, admit this important truth; and the Gospel establishes it no less strongly than the law. See <reference osisRef="Mat.6.26">Mat 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.10.29">Mat 10:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.30">Mat 10:30</reference>. To raise the mind of the prophet up to the first Mover of those events which strike and admonish us in all the revolutions which happen to individuals, families, and states, God shows him four wheels above the firmament, over which the emblem of Providence was placed on a throne. These wheels are a symbol of those perpetual revolutions, which are observed in the earth; and which, by turns, lift up and abase individuals and nations. They are of a prodigious height, to show that man cannot fathom or know all that is great, wonderful, and astonishing, in the ways of Providence. See <reference osisRef="Job.11.7">Job 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom 11:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Rom 11:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8">Isa 55:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.9">Isa 55:9</reference>. These wheels move themselves every way, and are full of eyes in the vast circle of their felloes. This shows, that all which God does he effects without pain; and that the eye of his wisdom ordereth all events. The wheels did not move of themselves; but they followed the impulse of the four living creatures; 'when the living creatures went, they went.' This shows that, in the government of the world, all the living creatures are subject to Providence; and that God subordinates the creatures one to another. He directs what those holy intelligences ought to do, who serve him as ministers, and are here represented by the four animals. And these intelligences, enlightened and supported by the Supreme Wisdom, contribute, as far as is suitable, to all that happens to mankind. The angels whom Ezekiel saw were in number four, in reference to the four cardinal points of the world; to show that their ministry extends every where, and that there is no part of the universe which the Providence of God does not govern in an immediate manner, or by the means of his ministers. The extraordinary shape of these angels, which appeared to the prophet in vision, is symbolical; for it is not to be supposed that those heavenly ministers are really thus formed. The 'four faces, wings, and arms of a man,' denote the sublime qualities of these immediate ministers of the Deity; qualities entirely essential to fill up the extent of their duty. The face of a man denotes their intelligence; of a lion, their intrepid courage; of an ox, their patience and perseverance in labor; and of an eagle, their great penetration, their sublime sight into heavenly things, and their readiness to rise up into all that is great and Divine. The 'wings being stretched out,' signifies that they are always ready to set forward, and run with rapidity wherever the commands of their great Master call them. The 'wings bent down,' are a symbol of that profound respect in which these heavenly ministers stand before the Lord of the universe. Under the wings there were men's arms, to show that zeal produces application and labor. Labour, without zeal, can never be supported; and zeal, without application, is only a hypocritical ardour, which amounts to nothing with that supreme Master who requires sincere homage from those who serve him. If God chose to make known to Ezekiel that his providence extends to all things, and that even in this life it often takes up the rod to chastise nations and individuals, he would also show beforehand that he wished not the destruction of the Jewish people, whom he was about to visit in his anger, but only its correction and amendment. This is signified by the 'precious metal,' which the prophet found unmelted in the midst of the fiery cloud. This cloud of fire, urged on by a whirlwind, and involving on all sides the metal, represented the judgments of God which were about to fall upon this rebellious nation, not to destroy, but to humble and purify it. Nothing is more proper than afflictions to bring men back to their duty. As fire purifies metals, so the paternal chastisements of God have a tendency to purify the soul and heart, if the man be not entirely incorrigible. The people upon whom God was about to pour the vials of his anger, were not worthy of his lenity. But that great God, who is firm in his promises, remembers the covenant of peace he had made with the patriarchs. This covenant is made sensible to the prophet under the image of a rainbow, which was round about him who appeared upon the throne. Every one knows, that this splendid phenomenon, which seems to join heaven and earth together, was given to Noah and his posterity as a symbol of the covenant which God then made with mankind, and by which he declared to them that the earth should undergo a deluge no more. Thus, the Pagans considered the Iris as the messenger of the gods. See Virgil, Aen. lib. 4 ver. 694. But whereas the rainbow to the Jews was a symbol of peace, the Iris of the Pagans was a messenger of trouble. On the sight of this bow, the symbol of grace, Ezekiel was to be encouraged; and persuaded that his people were not threatened with an utter destruction. The event fully justified all that the prophet had contemplated, with surprise, in this enigmatical picture. The Chaldeans, the rod of the Lord's just severity, ravaged Judea; the people were carried away captive; they groaned for seventy years in a foreign land; but they were protected in a miraculous manner against the bloody designs of the cruel Haman; and at length, favored with various decrees of the kings of Persia, they had permission, not only to return to their own country but also to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple.' See Dr. Dodd's notes on this place.  <chapter eID="Ezek.10"/> <div eID="gen31464" type="x-p"/>

entries.b21427f03329c21ccc830e569fb9c4ed5e309e94: <div eID="gen14859" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Burning of Jerusalem, and Withdrawal of the Glory of Jehovah from the Sanctuary</title> <div sID="gen14860" type="x-p"/> This chapter divides itself into two sections. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1-Ezek.10.8">Eze 10:1-8</reference> the prophet is shown how Jerusalem is to be burned with fire. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.9-Ezek.10.22">Eze 10:9-22</reference> he is shown how Jehovah will forsake His temple. <div eID="gen14860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14861" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1-Ezek.10.8">Eze 10:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen14861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14862" type="x-p"/> The angel scatters coals of fire over Jerusalem. - Eze 10:1.<hi type="italic">And I saw, and behold upon the firmament, which was above the cherubim, it was like sapphire-stone, to look at as the likeness of a throne; He appeared above them.</hi> Eze 10:2. <hi type="italic">And He spake to the man clothed in white linen, and said: Come between the wheels below the cherubim, and fill thy hollow hands with fire-coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city: and he came before my eyes.</hi> Eze 10:3. <hi type="italic">And the cherubim stood to the right of the house when the man came, and the cloud filled the inner court.</hi> Eze 10:4. <hi type="italic">And the glory of Jehovah had lifted itself up from the cherubim to the threshold of the house; and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was full of the splendour of the glory of Jehovah.</hi> Eze 10:5. <hi type="italic">And the noise of the wings of the cherubim was heard to the outer court, as the voice of the Almighty God when He speaketh.</hi> Eze 10:6. <hi type="italic">And it came to pass, when He commanded the man clothed in white linen, and said, Take fire from between the wheels, from between the cherubim, and he came and stood by the side of the wheel,</hi> Eze 10:7. <hi type="italic">That the cherub stretched out his hand between the cherubim to the fire, which was between the cherubim, and lifted (some) off and gave it into the hands of the man clothed in white linen. And he took it, and went out.</hi> Eze 10:8. <hi type="italic">And there appeared by the cherubim the likeness of a man’s hand under their wings.</hi> - <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1">Eze 10:1</reference> introduces the description of the second act of the judgment. According to <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3">Eze 9:3</reference>, Jehovah had come down from His throne above the cherubim to the threshold of the temple to issue His orders thence for the judgment upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference> He goes thither once more. Consequently He had resumed His seat above the cherubim in the meantime. This is expressed in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.1">Eze 10:1</reference>, not indeed in so many words, but indirectly or by implication. Ezekiel sees the theophany; and on the firmament above the cherubim, like sapphire-stone to look at, he beholds the likeness of a throne on which Jehovah appeared. To avoid giving too great prominence in this appearance of Jehovah to the bodily or human form, Ezekiel does not speak even here of the form of Jehovah, but simply of His throne, which he describes in the same manner as in Eze 1:26. אל stands for על according to the later usage of the language. It will never do to take אל in its literal sense, as Kliefoth does, and render the words: “Ezekiel saw it move away to the firmament;” for the object to ואראה והנּה is not יהוה or כּבוד , but the form of the throne sparkling in sapphire-stone; and this throne had not separated itself from the firmament above the cherubim, but Jehovah, or the glory of Jehovah, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3">Eze 9:3</reference>, had risen up from the cherubim, and moved away to the temple threshold. The כּ before מראה is not to be erased, as Hitzig proposes after the lxx, on the ground that it is not found in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.26">Eze 1:26</reference>; it is quite appropriate here. For the words do not affirm that Ezekiel saw the likeness of a throne like sapphire-stone; but that he saw something like sapphire-stone, like the appearance of the form of a throne. Ezekiel does not see Jehovah, or the glory of Jehovah, move away to the firmament, and then return to the throne. He simply sees once more the resemblance of a throne upon the firmament, and the Lord appearing thereon. The latter is indicated in נראה עליהם. These words are not to be taken in connection with 'כּמראה וגו, so as to form one sentence; but have been very properly separated by the <hi type="italic">athnach</hi> under כּסּא, and treated as an independent assertion. The subject to נראה might, indeed, be דּמוּת כּסּא, “the likeness of a throne appeared above the cherubim;” but in that case the words would form a pure tautology, as the fact of the throne becoming visible has already been mentioned in the preceding clause. The subject must therefore be Jehovah, as in the case of ויּאמר in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>, where there can be no doubt on the matter. Jehovah has resumed His throne, not “for the purpose of removing to a distance, because the courts of the temple have been defiled by dead bodies” (Hitzig), but because the object for which He left it has been attained. <div eID="gen14862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14863" type="x-p"/> He now commands the man clothed in white linen to go in between the wheels under the cherubim, and fill his hands with fire-coals from thence, and scatter them over the city (Jerusalem). This he did, so that Ezekiel could see it. According to this, it appears as if Jehovah had issued the command from His throne; but if we compare what follows, it is evident from <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference> that the glory of Jehovah had risen up again from the throne, and removed to the threshold of the temple, and that it was not till after the man in white linen had scattered the coals over the city that it left the threshold of the temple, and ascended once more up to the throne above the cherubim, so as to forsake the temple (Eze 10:18.). Consequently we can only understand <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2-Ezek.10.7">Eze 10:2-7</reference> as implying that Jehovah issued the command in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>, not from His throne, but from the threshold of the temple, and that He had therefore returned to the threshold of the temple for this purpose, and for the very same reason as in Eze 9:3. The possibility of interpreting the verses in this way is apparent from the fact that <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference> contains a summary of the whole of the contents of this section, and that <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3-Ezek.10.7">Eze 10:3-7</reference> simply furnish more minute explanations, or contain circumstantial clauses, which throw light upon the whole affair. This is obvious in the case of <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">Eze 10:3</reference>, from the form of the clause; and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.5">Eze 10:5</reference>, from the fact that in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.6">Eze 10:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.7">Eze 10:7</reference> the command (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>) is resumed, and the execution of it, which was already indicated in ויּבא לעיני (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>), more minutely described and carried forward in the closing words of the seventh verse, ויּקּח . הגּלגּל in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference> signifies the whirl or rotatory motion, i.e., the wheel-work, or the four ōphannim under the cherubim regarded as moving. The angel was to go in between these, and take coals out of the fire there, and scatter them over the city. “In the fire of God, the fire of His wrath, will kindle the fire for consuming the city” (Kliefoth). To depict the scene more clearly, Ezekiel observes in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">Eze 10:3</reference>, that at this moment the cherubim were standing to the right of the house, i.e., on the south or rather south-east of the temple house, on the south of the altar of burnt-offering. According to the Hebrew usage the right side as the southern side, and the prophet was in the inner court, whither, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>, the divine glory had taken him; and, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>, the seven angels had gone to the front of the altar, to receive the commands of the Lord. Consequently we have to picture to ourselves the cherubim as appearing in the neighbourhood of the altar, and then taking up their position to the south thereof, when the Lord returned to the threshold of the temple.
